title: What is cash accounting?
subtitle: Recognised by actual cash flow - simple but limited
openingQuestion: Cash accounting suits which type of user best?
openingOptions: Small businesses with few credit transactions, wanting simplicity
Multinational conglomerates that have many overseas subsidiaries abroad
explanation: Cash accounting only records when cash actually moves in or out, so it's very simple and suits small household businesses. The weakness shows immediately once there's buying or selling on credit: a month collecting a lot of old debt looks like a boom month, while a month prepaying a full year's rent looks like a loss-making month. Because profit jumps around based on the timing of cash flows rather than actual activity, any business past a small scale must move to accrual.

diagram.label: Only track cash in and out
But profit jumps with the timing of receipts and payments, not the actual period

realWorldExample.description: Small household businesses in Vietnam usually apply simple cash accounting - only recording actual receipts and payments - because their small scale doesn't require the added precision of accrual accounting.

quiz.question: Cash Accounting records:
options: When an invoice is issued to the customer
When the obligation to deliver arises
When the contract is signed and takes effect
When cash actually moves in or out
quiz.explanation: Issuing an invoice, incurring an obligation and signing a contract are all accrual triggers - each recognises the event before any money moves. Cash basis ignores all three and waits for the bank balance to change.

quiz.question: Who uses Cash Accounting?
options: Household businesses and very small companies
Companies listed on the stock exchange
Companies with foreign investment capital
Banks and other credit institutions
quiz.explanation: Small and simple → cash basis is enough. Large and complex → accrual is required.

quiz.question: The advantage of Cash Accounting is:
options: It reflects the true substance of the business
Simple, easy to understand, easy to verify
It's trusted by institutional investors
It's comparable across companies
quiz.explanation: The other three are accrual's advantages, not cash basis's: institutional investors and cross-company comparison both need matching, which cash basis does not provide. Its one real strength is that a bank statement is hard to dispute.

quiz.question: A problem with Cash Accounting is:
options: The actual cash balance is recorded incorrectly
It cannot calculate the tax due for the period
Credit sales aren't recognised as revenue
Depreciation expense ends up double-counted
quiz.explanation: Cash basis records the bank balance accurately - that is its whole point - and tax authorities accept it for small businesses. Depreciation never enters cash basis at all, so it cannot be double-counted. What it misses is the credit sale: goods delivered, revenue unrecorded.

quiz.question: A small company on cash basis shows 10 million profit. In reality:
options: Exactly 10 million, because cash in equals profit
Always lower than 10 million after adjustment
Always higher than 10 million due to depreciation
Could differ, depending on AR, AP and CapEx
quiz.explanation: Neither direction is guaranteed. Rising receivables push cash profit below accrual profit, while unpaid supplier bills push it above; depreciation does not enter cash basis at all, so it cannot force the figure higher.

quiz.question: Why doesn't everyone use accrual?
options: Accrual is much more complex and costly
Accrual applies only in a narrow set of cases
Accrual raises the corporate tax owed
Accrual is only for foreign companies
quiz.explanation: Accrual is not restricted in scope, nor reserved for foreign companies - it is the global standard. Nor does it change the tax eventually owed, only the period the profit lands in. What stops a small business adopting it is the bookkeeping cost.

quiz.question: A small company borrowing from a bank should prepare:
options: Accrual, because the bank needs standardised figures
Cash basis, because it is simpler and more honest to read
Both books at once so the bank can cross-check itself
No preparation needed, the bank only checks bank statements
quiz.explanation: Cash basis is not more honest, only more literal - it leaves out the receivables and obligations a lender has to see. Keeping two sets of books invites exactly the inconsistency banks screen for, and bank statements alone show no profitability.

keyTakeaways: Cash accounting: recognised when cash actually moves in/out
Disadvantage: no matching, easily distorts profit

practicePrompt.question: A small household business sells 50 million of goods to a customer in June, but the customer agrees to pay in August. If this business uses cash accounting, how much revenue will the June report recognise from this transaction?
options: Recognise the full 50 million in June, exactly as accrual accounting would
Zero - cash accounting only books the revenue when the money actually lands, so that is August
25 million - recognising half right away and the remaining half in August
It cannot be determined without information about the corresponding cost of goods sold
practicePrompt.explanation: Cash accounting recognises when cash actually moves in/out, regardless of when the transaction occurred - so June will record 0 dong of revenue from this transaction, with the full 50 million only recognised in August, when the cash actually reaches the account.

summary.keyIdea: Cash accounting: recognised when cash actually moves in/out
summary.commonMistake: Reading a concept as a phrase to memorise rather than a principle to apply to real decisions.

application.title: Try keeping cash-accounting books for a week
application.message: Over the next 7 days, only record the amounts of cash that actually move into/out of your wallet or account (not amounts promised or not yet paid) to experience how cash accounting works.
application.secondary: You'll find it simple but it misses obligations not yet due.

sections.text: Cash Accounting is the opposite of accrual accounting: it only recognises revenue and expenses when cash actually moves into or out of the business. Simple, intuitive, but clearly limited as a business grows in scale.

For a small household business, a grocery store, or a freelancer, cash accounting fits well because there are few credit transactions and a simple business cycle - sell and collect cash right away, buy and pay cash right away. No need to track complex receivables and payables, and the books are easy to understand and easy to reconcile against the actual bank balance.
The limits as a business grows

The problem with cash accounting is that it allows - whether accidentally or deliberately - profit to be distorted between periods. A business can delay paying an expense into the next month to make this month's profit look better, or ask customers to pay early to pull revenue into the current period. Without a matching principle, two adjacent reporting periods may not accurately reflect true operating performance, making it hard for investors to compare.

items: Cash accounting fits: sole proprietorships, SMEs with few credit transactions, simple service industries
Cash accounting doesn't fit: businesses with credit sales/purchases, depreciable assets, long-term contracts
IFRS/VAS standards require accrual for public listed companies - cash accounting is only for internal use or very small businesses

sections.label: A real-world example
sections.text: A small household grocery store in Vietnam keeps simple books: today it sold this much cash, today it paid this much cash for new stock - that's exactly cash accounting. But if that store grows into a mini-supermarket chain with hundreds of suppliers on credit, cash accounting will no longer be enough to reflect the true financial picture.

left.label: Cash accounting
left.text: Simple, easy to understand, suits small businesses with few credit transactions - but easily distorts profit by period

right.label: Accrual accounting
right.text: More complex but reflects true operating performance, mandatory for listed businesses

lines: Cash accounting is a good starting point for understanding cash flow, but not enough for in-depth financial analysis.
The larger a business gets and the more credit transactions it has, the more it needs to switch to accrual accounting.
Understanding the difference between the two methods helps you correctly read the meaning behind every accounting number.
